title.en: LSTM & GRU: Solving the Memory Problem

description.en: Master LSTM cells with forget, input, and output gates, and understand GRU as a simpler alternative for long-range dependencies.
description.ta: forget, input, output gates உடன் LSTM செல்களை கற்றுக்கொண்டு, நீண்ட தூர சார்புகளுக்கான எளிய மாற்றாக GRU-ஐ புரிந்துகொள்ளுங்கள்.

story_variants.en:
## Vaathiyaar's Smart Notebook

Vaathiyaar shows two notebooks. "The old notebook (vanilla RNN) fades after a few pages. This smart notebook (LSTM) has gates — it decides what to remember, what to forget, and what to write next."

### LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# LSTM layer
lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=10, hidden_size=32, num_layers=2,
               batch_first=True, dropout=0.2)

# Input: batch=4, seq_len=20, features=10
x = torch.randn(4, 20, 10)

# Forward pass returns output, (hidden_state, cell_state)
output, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(x)

print(f'Output: {output.shape}')  # [4, 20, 32]
print(f'Hidden: {h_n.shape}')     # [2, 4, 32] - 2 layers
print(f'Cell:   {c_n.shape}')     # [2, 4, 32]
```

### GRU: Gated Recurrent Unit (Simpler)

```python
gru = nn.GRU(input_size=10, hidden_size=32, num_layers=2,
             batch_first=True, dropout=0.2)

output, h_n = gru(x)  # No cell state — only hidden state
print(f'GRU Output: {output.shape}')  # [4, 20, 32]
print(f'GRU Hidden: {h_n.shape}')     # [2, 4, 32]
```

### Sequence Classification with LSTM

```python
class SentimentLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, hidden_dim, num_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(embed_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers=2,
                           batch_first=True, dropout=0.3, bidirectional=True)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim * 2, num_classes)  # *2 for bidirectional
    
    def forward(self, x):
        embedded = self.embedding(x)          # [batch, seq] -> [batch, seq, embed]
        output, (h_n, c_n) = self.lstm(embedded)
        # Concatenate forward and backward final hidden states
        hidden = torch.cat((h_n[-2], h_n[-1]), dim=1)
        return self.fc(hidden)

model = SentimentLSTM(vocab_size=10000, embed_dim=128, hidden_dim=64, num_classes=2)
```

> **LSTM vs GRU:** LSTM has 3 gates + cell state (more powerful, more params). GRU has 2 gates (faster, often comparable accuracy).
story_variants.ta:
## வாத்தியாரின் ஸ்மார்ட் குறிப்பேடு

வாத்தியார் இரண்டு குறிப்பேடுகளைக் காட்டுகிறார். "பழைய குறிப்பேடு (vanilla RNN) சில பக்கங்களுக்குப் பிறகு மறைந்துவிடும். இந்த ஸ்மார்ட் குறிப்பேடு (LSTM) gates கொண்டுள்ளது — என்ன நினைவில் வைக்க, என்ன மறக்க, அடுத்து என்ன எழுத என்பதை தீர்மானிக்கிறது."

explanation.en: 2-layer LSTM: 10 input features, 32-dim hidden/cell state per layer
LSTM returns output AND (hidden_state, cell_state). Cell state is LSTM's long-term memory
Final hidden state for each layer. h_n[-1] is the last layer's final hidden state
Cell state: the 'conveyor belt' of long-term memory. Unique to LSTM (GRU lacks this)
GRU: simpler than LSTM with only 2 gates (reset and update). No separate cell state
Convert word indices to dense vectors. vocab_size words, each becomes embed_dim-dimensional
Process sequence both forward and backward. Doubles hidden size in output
Concatenate forward and backward final hidden states for classification
Classifier takes concatenated bidirectional hidden state (*2 for both directions)
LSTM has 4x more parameters than vanilla RNN due to 4 weight matrices (3 gates + candidate)

left.label: LSTM
left.content:
3 gates (forget, input, output)
Separate cell state
More parameters
Better for long sequences

right.label: GRU
right.content:
2 gates (reset, update)
No cell state
Fewer parameters
Faster training, often similar accuracy

instruction.en: PyTorch cannot run in this sandbox, so this is the numpy version of what PyTorch does under the hood. Write one LSTM time step and run it over a sequence. `lstm_cell(x, h_prev, c_prev, W, U, b)`: compute z = x @ W + h_prev @ U + b and split it into 4 equal parts in PyTorch's gate order i, f, g, o; i, f and o go through sigmoid, g through tanh; then c = f * c_prev + i * g and h = o * tanh(c); return (h, c). `run_lstm(sequence, W, U, b)` starts with h and c as zeros (size = U.shape[0]), applies lstm_cell to every time step and returns the final (h, c). The forget gate f is what lets the cell state remember across many steps.
instruction.ta: இந்த sandbox-ல் PyTorch இயங்காது, எனவே இது PyTorch உள்ளே செய்வதன் numpy பதிப்பு. ஒரு LSTM time step-ஐ எழுதி அதை ஒரு sequence மீது இயக்குங்கள். `lstm_cell(x, h_prev, c_prev, W, U, b)`: z = x @ W + h_prev @ U + b கணக்கிட்டு, அதை PyTorch-இன் gate வரிசையில் i, f, g, o என 4 சம பகுதிகளாகப் பிரியுங்கள்; i, f, o sigmoid வழியாகவும், g tanh வழியாகவும் செல்லும்; பிறகு c = f * c_prev + i * g, h = o * tanh(c); (h, c) திருப்புங்கள். `run_lstm(sequence, W, U, b)` h, c இரண்டையும் பூஜ்யங்களாகத் (அளவு = U.shape[0]) தொடங்கி, ஒவ்வொரு time step-க்கும் lstm_cell-ஐப் பயன்படுத்தி இறுதி (h, c)-ஐத் திருப்புகிறது. Forget gate f தான் cell state பல steps முழுவதும் நினைவில் வைத்திருக்க உதவுகிறது.

    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

    # 3. sigmoid for i, f, o; tanh for g
    # 4. c = f * c_prev + i * g;  h = o * tanh(c)
    pass


def run_lstm(sequence, W, U, b):
    # start from zero h and c, loop over the time steps, return the final (h, c)
    pass


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
input_size, hidden_size = 1, 4
W = rng.standard_normal((input_size, 4 * hidden_size)) * 0.5
U = rng.standard_normal((hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size)) * 0.5
b = np.zeros(4 * hidden_size)

sequence = np.sin(np.linspace(0, 3, 10)).reshape(10, 1)   # a short sine wave, one value per step
result = run_lstm(sequence, W, U, b)
if result is None:
    print("run_lstm() returned None")
else:
    h, c = result
    print("final hidden state:", np.round(h, 4))
    print("final cell state:  ", np.round(c, 4))

i, f, o = sigmoid(i), sigmoid(f), sigmoid(o) and g = np.tanh(g)
c = f * c_prev + i * g; h = o * np.tanh(c); return h, c

practice_challenges.test_code:
import numpy as np


def _sig(v):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-v))


def _ref_cell(x, h, c, W, U, b):
    z = x @ W + h @ U + b
    H = h.shape[-1]
    i, f, g, o = _sig(z[..., :H]), _sig(z[..., H:2*H]), np.tanh(z[..., 2*H:3*H]), _sig(z[..., 3*H:])
    c2 = f * c + i * g
    return o * np.tanh(c2), c2


_rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
_W = _rng.standard_normal((2, 12)); _U = _rng.standard_normal((3, 12)); _b = _rng.standard_normal(12)
_x = _rng.standard_normal(2); _h = _rng.standard_normal(3); _c = _rng.standard_normal(3)
_out = lstm_cell(_x, _h, _c, _W, _U, _b)
assert isinstance(_out, tuple) and len(_out) == 2, "lstm_cell must return (h, c)"
_rh, _rc = _ref_cell(_x, _h, _c, _W, _U, _b)
assert np.allclose(_out[1], _rc), "cell state must be c = f * c_prev + i * g (gate order i, f, g, o)"
assert np.allclose(_out[0], _rh), "hidden state must be h = o * tanh(c)"
_bias = np.zeros(12); _bias[0:3] = -20; _bias[3:6] = 20; _bias[9:12] = 20
_h2, _c2 = lstm_cell(np.zeros(2), np.zeros(3), _c, np.zeros((2, 12)), np.zeros((3, 12)), _bias)
assert np.allclose(_c2, _c, atol=1e-6), "with the forget gate open (f=1) and input gate shut (i=0) the cell state must be kept unchanged"
_seq = _rng.standard_normal((5, 2))
_res = run_lstm(_seq, _W, _U, _b)
assert isinstance(_res, tuple) and len(_res) == 2, "run_lstm must return the final (h, c)"
_eh, _ec = np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3)
for _xt in _seq:
    _eh, _ec = _ref_cell(_xt, _eh, _ec, _W, _U, _b)
assert np.allclose(_res[0], _eh) and np.allclose(_res[1], _ec), "run_lstm must start from zeros and apply lstm_cell to every time step in order"
print("All LSTM tests passed!")

q.en: How does GRU differ from LSTM?

en: GRU has 2 gates and no separate cell state, making it simpler
ta: GRU-க்கு 2 gates உள்ளன, தனி cell state இல்லை, எளிமையானது

en: Processes the sequence both forward and backward, doubling the hidden state size
ta: வரிசையை முன்னும் பின்னும் செயலாக்கி, hidden state அளவை இரட்டிப்பாக்குகிறது

under_the_hood.summary: A stacked LSTM passes each layer's hidden states up to the next layer at every time step and returns the top layer's outputs plus each layer's final (h, c); a GRU does the same job with two gates and no separate cell state.

steps.title: Shapes of a two-layer LSTM
steps.body: nn.LSTM(input_size=10, hidden_size=32, num_layers=2, batch_first=True, dropout=0.2) on x of shape (4, 20, 10) returns output (4, 20, 32), the top layer's hidden state at every step, and h_n and c_n of shape (2, 4, 32), the last step's states for each of the 2 layers. output[:, -1] equals h_n[-1].

steps.title: Stacking: layer 2 reads layer 1
steps.body: At each time step, layer 1's hidden state becomes layer 2's input. The dropout=0.2 argument applies dropout to those connections between layers (not to the last layer's output), which is why PyTorch warns if you set dropout with num_layers=1.

props.caption: One time step through two stacked layers

steps.title: The GRU update, worked
steps.body: A GRU computes an update gate z and a reset gate r with sigmoids, a candidate n = tanh(W x + r * (U h_prev)), and blends: h = (1 - z) * n + z * h_prev. With h_prev = 0.8, z = 0.7 and n = -0.2: h = 0.3 x (-0.2) + 0.7 x 0.8 = 0.50. A z near 1 copies the old state forward almost untouched, which preserves memory and gradients.

steps.title: Three gates' worth of weights, not four
steps.body: Each gate needs its own input and hidden weights. For input 10 and hidden 32, one LSTM layer has 4 x (32 x 10 + 32 x 32 + 64) = 5,632 parameters, a GRU layer 3 x (...) = 4,224, a quarter fewer. GRUs are a bit faster and often just as accurate; LSTMs' separate cell can help on very long dependencies.

steps.title: Bidirectional and packed sequences
steps.body: bidirectional=True runs a second LSTM from the end of the sequence backwards and concatenates both directions, doubling output features to 64. For batches of different-length sequences, pack_padded_sequence lets the LSTM skip padding steps so the final states come from each sequence's real last token.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Know the shapes, (batch, time, hidden) for outputs and (layers, batch, hidden) for final states, and the gate arithmetic. LSTM and GRU differ in bookkeeping, not in purpose: both keep a gated memory path through time.
